newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: French, Dutch play down talk of growing rift.
newsitem.headline: French, Dutch play down talk of growing rift.

text.p: France and The Netherlands dampened talk on Friday that a long-standing rift over drugs had spilled over into the Dutch central bank chief's job prospects.
European Union leaders at a summit in the Irish capital confirmed Wim Duisenberg as the next president of the EU's European Monetary Institute (EMI) from July 1, 1997.

As the EMI is the forerunner of the European Central Bank, which is due to run monetary policy after economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, Duisenberg, Europe's longest-serving central bank chief, was widely tipped to head the ECB and oversee the birth of the planned single currency.
But French President Jacques Chirac told fellow EU leaders that the choice of Duisenberg as EMI chief did not mean he would automatically head the new central bank.

"The decision on the nomination does not prejudge the presidency of the European Central Bank," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told a news briefing. "We will be in a new phase and no doubt there will have to be a new team and new personalities."
Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm told Dutch reporters in Dublin that he thought Chirac was speaking alone when making his comments about Duisenberg's prospects.
"The other leaders listened to Chirac, but...I suspect they did not share his opinion. But then France has a thing about The Netherlands," he was quoted as saying.

French diplomats dismissed the idea that Chirac's remark was a snub to Duisenberg, saying that the top ECB post was one of the most important European posts coming up and nothing should be taken for granted so far ahead of time.
France has argued for some political control over the planned ECB rather than seeing it run by technocrats along the lines of the German Bundesbank, which is closely linked to the Dutch central bank.
Jan Rood, European affairs adviser at the Hague-based Clingendael Institute for International Relations, doubted a link between Chirac's remarks and the drugs dispute.
"It didn't surprise me, but if there is a link, then they (France) are going too far," he said.
Dutch diplomats said the Netherlands had never assumed that Duisenberg would automatically move from the EMI to head up the ECB. "We never drew any conclusions from his appointment," one said.
One EU source said there could be several candidates for the post of ECB chief.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet has long been believed to be interested in heading the ECB, but it is unclear how much support he has with Chirac.
Dutch morale has been mauled in recent years as several Dutch candidates have missed out on high-profile international posts, leaving a national vulnerability to disappointment.
After a long run of failures for top posts, former Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers last year looked certain to be chosen as NATO Secretary-General until Washington vetoed his candidacy.
Duisenberg, 61, has steered the Netherlands to successive years of growth and strong money and the Dutch economy is widely seen as a model for Europe's economic future.

The French and Dutch have been at loggerheads over Dutch drug laws which, Paris protests, have led to thousands of young French "tourists" flocking to The Netherlands to buy cheap and readily available narcotics.
Drugs are illegal in the Netherlands, but sales of modest amounts of soft drugs from "coffee-shops" are allowed under a progressive 20-year drugs experiment.
